meta.description: Master ISTQB CTFL v4.0.1 question bank for this repo. Append-only history of every question ever generated for a timed mock exam (see question-bank/README.md). Grounded in resources/ISTQB_CTFL_Syllabus_v4.0.1.pdf / resources/istqb-ctfl-syllabus-v4.0.1.extracted.txt.

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements:

I. When static testing identifies a defect, debugging still requires a reproduction step before the defect can be fixed.
II. Confirmation testing that follows debugging after a dynamic-testing failure is preferably performed by the same person who ran the original failing test.

Which is correct?

options.A: Only I is correct
options.B: Only II is correct
options.C: Both I and II are correct
options.D: Neither I nor II is correct

questions.why_correct: The syllabus explicitly states that when static testing finds a defect, there is no need for reproduction or diagnosis, since static testing finds the defect directly without ever causing a failure. Reproduction is only needed for defects behind a dynamic-testing failure. It also explicitly recommends the same person who performed the initial test preferably do the confirmation testing.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — I is false, not true.
option_notes.B: Correct — I is false (static testing needs no reproduction step), II is true.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — I is false.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — II is true.

questions.distractor_note: Statement I is built to sound reasonable because 'debugging' is generically associated with reproduce-diagnose-fix, but that three-step process is specifically the *dynamic*-testing-triggered debugging process. Static testing skips reproduction/diagnosis entirely because it finds the defect directly.
questions.alt_wording: Exam may phrase this as 'what must happen before a defect found by a review can be fixed' (answer: nothing extra — no reproduction needed) or 'who should ideally re-run a previously failed test after a fix'.

questions.question: Under deadline pressure, a developer copy-pastes a validation function but forgets to update a variable reference. The resulting source code now contains an incorrect boundary check. Months later, in production, a customer enters a value at exactly that boundary and the checkout page crashes. What is the correct mapping of terms, in order of occurrence?

options.A: Root cause = time pressure; Error = the mistaken copy-paste edit; Defect = the incorrect code; Failure = the checkout page crashing
options.B: Error = time pressure; Defect = the mistaken copy-paste edit; Failure = the incorrect code; Root cause = the checkout page crashing
options.C: Defect = time pressure; Error = the incorrect code; Root cause = the mistaken copy-paste edit; Failure = the checkout page crashing
options.D: Failure = time pressure; Root cause = the incorrect code; Error = the checkout page crashing; Defect = the mistaken copy-paste edit

questions.why_correct: The syllabus chain is: humans make errors (mistakes) → which produce defects (faults, bugs) → which may result in failures when executed. Time pressure is a typical example of a root cause behind the human error. So: root cause (time pressure) causes the error (the mistaken edit), which produces the defect (the wrong code), which results in the failure (the crash) once executed with the triggering input.

option_notes.A: Correct — matches the syllabus's error → defect → failure chain with time pressure as the root cause behind the error.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — shuffles every term one step out of place; time pressure is a root cause, not an error itself.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — reverses defect and root cause entirely.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — places the observable failure (the crash) as if it were an error, and the root cause as if it were the code defect.

questions.alt_wording: May appear as 'which of these is the root cause vs. the defect' in a short narrative, or ask you to identify only one of the four terms from a scenario.

questions.question: During a test cycle, 70% of all logged defects are traced back to just two of the system's twenty modules. Which testing principle BEST explains why focusing additional test effort on those two modules is a reasonable response?

options.A: Exhaustive testing is impossible
options.B: Defects cluster together
options.C: Tests wear out
options.D: Absence-of-defects fallacy

questions.why_correct: The 'defects cluster together' principle states that a small number of components usually contain most of the discovered defects or are responsible for most operational failures — an illustration of the Pareto principle. This directly matches the 70%-in-two-modules scenario and is an important input for risk-based testing.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — that principle is about the infeasibility of testing every possible combination, not about defect distribution across modules.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — that principle is about repeated tests becoming less effective over time, unrelated to clustering.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — that principle is about verification passing not guaranteeing the system meets real user needs, unrelated to this scenario.

questions.alt_wording: May be phrased as 'the Pareto principle applied to testing' or 'why should risk-based testing pay special attention to historically defect-prone components'.

questions.question: All of the following are among the seven testing principles described in the syllabus EXCEPT:

options.A: Early testing saves time and money
options.B: Testing is context dependent
options.C: Automating all test cases eliminates the need for further manual testing
options.D: Exhaustive testing is impossible

questions.why_correct: There is no such principle. The seven principles are: (1) testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects; (2) exhaustive testing is impossible; (3) early testing saves time and money; (4) defects cluster together; (5) tests wear out; (6) testing is context dependent; (7) absence-of-defects fallacy. None of them claim automation removes the need for manual testing — in fact this contradicts the syllabus's general position (see chapter 6) that manual testing, especially from the user's perspective, is still needed even with high automation.

option_notes.A: This IS a real principle — not the answer to this EXCEPT question.
option_notes.B: This IS a real principle — not the answer.
option_notes.C: Correct answer — this is not one of the seven principles, and it's actually a misconception the syllabus argues against elsewhere.
option_notes.D: This IS a real principle — not the answer.

questions.distractor_note: This option is tempting because it sounds like something the syllabus's automation section could say, but it inverts chapter 6's actual message: automation reduces repetitive manual work but does not eliminate the need for manual testing.
questions.alt_wording: May ask 'which of the following is NOT one of the seven testing principles' with different wrong-principle wording each time — always re-check against the canonical list of seven.

questions.question: A test manager wants to know, for every requirement in the specification, whether it is covered by at least one test case, and wants to know the residual risk remaining in the product before release. Which testware property is she relying on?

options.A: Traceability between the test basis, testware, and test results
options.B: The whole team approach
options.C: Static analysis
options.D: Test case prioritization

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states that traceability of test cases to requirements can verify that requirements are covered by test cases, and traceability of test results to risks can be used to evaluate the level of residual risk in a test object — exactly the two things described.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — a team collaboration practice, unrelated to coverage/risk tracing.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — a static-testing technique using tools, not a coverage/traceability mechanism.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — about ordering test execution, not about measuring coverage or residual risk.

questions.alt_wording: May describe traceability indirectly as 'being able to show which requirement each test case belongs to' or 'assessing product quality, process capability and project progress against business goals'.

questions.topic: Whole Team Approach vs. Independence of Testing
questions.question: A payments company is building a new internal admin dashboard, and separately, the flight-control software for a medical infusion pump. Which statement BEST reflects appropriate use of the whole team approach versus test independence for these two projects?

options.A: Both projects should use the whole team approach, since it always produces the highest-quality software
options.B: The admin dashboard can reasonably use the whole team approach for shared quality ownership; the infusion pump, being safety-critical, likely needs a high degree of independent testing instead
options.C: The infusion pump should use the whole team approach, since developers understand their own code best; the dashboard needs independent testers because it is customer-facing
options.D: Independence of testing and the whole team approach are the same practice applied at different test levels

questions.why_correct: The syllabus notes the whole team approach may not always be appropriate — for instance in safety-critical situations, where a high level of test independence may be needed instead. A low-risk internal dashboard is a reasonable fit for the whole team approach (shared ownership, co-location, synergy); a safety-critical medical device is exactly the kind of context where independent testing's benefit (recognizing different kinds of failures/defects due to a different background and less author bias) matters most.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — the syllabus explicitly says the whole team approach is not always appropriate, e.g., in safety-critical contexts.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — reverses the two projects' appropriate approaches.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — they are two different, sometimes competing, practices; independence is about who tests, the whole team approach is about shared responsibility for quality.

questions.alt_wording: May ask you to pick the project type that most needs 'a high level of independence' or to identify a drawback of the whole team approach in a safety-critical context.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of DevOps FROM THE TESTING PERSPECTIVE, according to the syllabus?

options.A: It removes the need for a dedicated test environment
options.B: Continuous integration promotes shift left by encouraging developers to submit code accompanied by component tests and static analysis
options.C: It guarantees zero regression defects in production
options.D: It eliminates the need for manual, user-perspective testing entirely

questions.why_correct: This is one of the syllabus's explicitly listed testing-perspective DevOps benefits: CI promotes shift left in testing by encouraging developers to submit high-quality code accompanied by component tests and static analysis.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — DevOps helps establish stable test environments through automation; it doesn't remove the need for one.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — DevOps minimizes regression risk through automated regression tests at scale; it never 'guarantees' zero defects, which would also contradict the absence-of-defects fallacy principle.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — the syllabus explicitly says manual testing, especially from the user's perspective, will still be needed even with a high level of automated testing.

questions.alt_wording: May ask to identify a DevOps risk instead (e.g., 'the pipeline must be defined and maintained', 'test automation requires additional resources') — read carefully whether the question asks for a benefit or a risk.

questions.question: A cross-functional team wants acceptance criteria expressed in a natural-language Given/When/Then format that non-technical stakeholders can read and that can be automatically translated into executable tests. Which test-first approach are they using?

options.A: Test-Driven Development (TDD)
options.B: Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD)
options.C: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)
options.D: Exploratory testing

questions.why_correct: BDD specifically expresses the desired behavior of an application using test cases written in a simple natural-language form — usually the Given/When/Then format — that stakeholders can understand, and these are then translated into executable tests.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — TDD directs coding through developer-written test cases before the code; it's not about natural-language stakeholder-readable acceptance criteria.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — ATDD derives tests from acceptance criteria as part of system design; Given/When/Then specifically is the hallmark of BDD, not ATDD generically.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — exploratory testing is an experience-based technique with no test-first, natural-language specification involved.

questions.distractor_note: ATDD is a tempting choice because it's also a test-first, acceptance-criteria-driven approach — but the specific Given/When/Then natural-language format called out by name in the syllabus belongs to BDD.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to match TDD/ATDD/BDD to a one-line description without naming the technique, or ask which one 'directs the coding through test cases instead of extensive software design' (that one is TDD).

questions.question: A team has finished testing each microservice in isolation. They now want to verify that Service A correctly calls Service B's API and correctly interprets its response, without yet involving any external third-party services. Which test level are they performing?

options.A: Component testing
options.B: Component integration testing
options.C: System integration testing
options.D: Acceptance testing

questions.why_correct: Component integration testing (also known as unit integration testing) focuses on testing the interfaces and interactions between components — exactly Service A calling Service B within the same system, before any external/third-party systems are involved.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — that's testing each component/microservice in isolation, which is described as already finished in the scenario.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — system integration testing is about interfaces between the system under test and OTHER systems/external services, not between two internal components.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — acceptance testing is about validating the whole system meets user/business needs, unrelated to inter-component API calls.

questions.distractor_note: System integration testing is the classic distractor here because it also involves 'interfaces' — the distinguishing detail is whether the interacting parties are internal components of the same system (component integration testing) or the system under test and an external system/service (system integration testing).
questions.alt_wording: May describe this as 'checking two internal modules talk to each other correctly' vs. 'checking the system talks correctly to an external payment gateway' (the latter is system integration testing).

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements about a defect fix:

I. Regression testing confirms that the specific reported defect no longer occurs.
II. Confirmation testing may be restricted, under time or budget pressure, to just re-exercising the steps that reproduced the original failure and checking it no longer occurs.

Which is correct?

options.A: Only I is correct
options.B: Only II is correct
options.C: Both I and II are correct
options.D: Neither I nor II is correct

questions.why_correct: Statement I reverses the two concepts: confirming the specific reported defect no longer occurs is confirmation testing's job, not regression testing's (regression testing checks that the change hasn't caused adverse consequences ELSEWHERE). Statement II is directly from the syllabus: when time or money is short, confirmation testing might be restricted to simply exercising the steps that reproduce the failure and checking it does not occur.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — I incorrectly swaps confirmation testing's job onto regression testing.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — I is false.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — II is true.

questions.distractor_note: This is one of the most common ISTQB exam traps: confirmation testing = 'did THIS defect get fixed?'; regression testing = 'did fixing it break something else?'. Statement I is written to sound plausible by using the word 'confirms', priming you toward confirmation testing's actual definition.
questions.alt_wording: Often appears as a direct definition-swap question: 'which testing type re-runs a previously failed test to check a specific fix?' (confirmation) vs. 'which testing type checks that unrelated areas still work after a change?' (regression).

questions.question: A company migrates its production database from an on-premises server to a cloud platform, with no functional changes to the application itself. According to the syllabus's classification of maintenance testing triggers, this is BEST classified as:

options.A: A modification, specifically a planned enhancement
options.B: An upgrade or migration of the operational environment
options.C: A retirement trigger
options.D: Not a maintenance testing trigger, since no application code changed

questions.why_correct: The syllabus classifies maintenance testing triggers into modifications (planned enhancements, corrective changes, hot fixes), upgrades or migrations of the operational environment (e.g., platform changes, which can require tests of the new environment and of data conversion), and retirement. Moving to a new cloud platform is exactly an upgrade/migration of the operational environment.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — modifications are about changes to the software itself (features/fixes), not a platform migration.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — retirement is about an application reaching end-of-life, not a platform move.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — environment migrations are explicitly one of the three trigger categories and still require testing (of the new environment and of data conversion).

questions.alt_wording: May describe 'data conversion testing when migrating from one application to another' or 'testing restore/retrieval after long-term archiving' (both also maintenance-testing scenarios, the latter under retirement).

questions.question: All of the following are genuine differences between static testing and dynamic testing EXCEPT:

options.A: Static testing can be applied to non-executable work products, while dynamic testing can only be applied to executable ones
options.B: Static testing finds defects directly, while dynamic testing causes failures whose defects are found through subsequent analysis
options.C: Static testing can measure quality characteristics not dependent on code execution (e.g., maintainability), while dynamic testing measures characteristics that depend on execution (e.g., performance efficiency)
options.D: Static testing and dynamic testing can never both detect the same underlying defect type

questions.why_correct: The syllabus says static and dynamic testing 'can both lead to the detection of defects', with some defect types findable only by one or the other — it never claims their defect-finding coverage is fully disjoint. The other three options are direct, accurate syllabus statements about their differences.

option_notes.A: This IS a genuine, syllabus-stated difference — not the answer.
option_notes.B: This IS a genuine, syllabus-stated difference — not the answer.
option_notes.C: This IS a genuine, syllabus-stated difference — not the answer.
option_notes.D: Correct answer — overstates the actual relationship; some defect types can be found by either approach.

questions.alt_wording: May ask 'which statement about static vs. dynamic testing is FALSE' instead of using EXCEPT — same trap, watch for the negation.

questions.question: During a formal review meeting, one participant is responsible for collating anomalies raised by each reviewer and logging the decisions made about them, while a different participant manages the meeting's timing and ensures everyone can speak freely. What are these two roles called, respectively?

options.A: Reviewer, then Author
options.B: Scribe, then Moderator
options.C: Review leader, then Manager
options.D: Moderator, then Scribe

questions.why_correct: The scribe (recorder) collates anomalies from reviewers and records review information such as decisions and new anomalies. The moderator (facilitator) ensures the effective running of review meetings, including mediation, time management, and a safe environment for open discussion.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — neither description matches a reviewer (who just performs reviews) or the author (who created and fixes the work product).
option_notes.C: Incorrect — the review leader takes overall responsibility for organizing the review (who/when/where); the manager decides what is reviewed and provides resources — neither matches the two descriptions given.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — the two roles are swapped relative to their descriptions.

questions.alt_wording: May instead describe the manager ('decides what is to be reviewed and provides resources') or the author ('creates and fixes the work product') and ask you to name the role.

questions.question: In which review type does the syllabus explicitly state that the author cannot act as the review leader or the scribe?

options.A: Informal review
options.B: Walkthrough
options.C: Technical review
options.D: Inspection

questions.why_correct: Inspections are the most formal review type and follow the complete generic review process; the syllabus explicitly states that in inspections, the author cannot act as the review leader or scribe — a restriction unique to inspections among the four listed review types.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — informal reviews have no defined process or formal output at all, so no such role restriction is specified.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — a walkthrough is actually LED BY THE AUTHOR, the opposite constraint.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — a technical review is led by a moderator, but the syllabus does not state this author restriction for it.
option_notes.D: Correct.

questions.distractor_note: Walkthrough is a strong distractor precisely because it also involves the author closely — but there the author actively LEADS the session, which is the opposite of being barred from a leadership/recording role, as in inspections.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which review type is 'led by the author' (walkthrough) or which has 'finding the maximum number of anomalies' as its main objective (inspection).

questions.question: A tester designs a test case purely from a requirements document, with no knowledge of how the feature is implemented internally. If the implementation changes later but the required behavior stays the same, the test case remains valid. Which category of test technique does this describe?

options.A: White-box (structure-based) test technique
options.B: Black-box (specification-based) test technique
options.C: Experience-based test technique
options.D: Static test technique

questions.why_correct: Black-box test techniques are based on an analysis of the specified behavior of the test object without reference to its internal structure, so test cases are independent of implementation — if the implementation changes but required behavior stays the same, the test cases remain useful. This is stated almost verbatim in the syllabus.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — white-box techniques are based on internal structure, so they can only be created after (and are dependent on) the design/implementation.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — experience-based techniques rely on tester knowledge/experience, not purely on a specification document.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — 'static' is a testing category (execution vs. no execution), not one of the three test-technique categories (black-box/white-box/experience-based).

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to distinguish the three technique categories directly, e.g., 'which technique category's effectiveness depends heavily on the tester's skill' (experience-based).

questions.question: A loyalty-tier field accepts an integer number of points and classifies customers as: Bronze (0–999), Silver (1000–4999), Gold (5000 or more). Negative numbers are rejected as invalid input. Using Equivalence Partitioning with Each Choice coverage, what is the MINIMUM number of test cases needed to achieve 100% coverage of all identified partitions?

options.A: 2 test cases
options.B: 3 test cases
options.C: 4 test cases
options.D: 6 test cases

questions.why_correct: There are 4 partitions here: 3 valid (Bronze 0–999, Silver 1000–4999, Gold >=5000) and 1 invalid (negative numbers). In EP, coverage is the number of partitions exercised by at least one test case divided by the total number of partitions; one test case per partition is sufficient (a value from one partition is assumed to be handled the same way as any other value in that partition). So the minimum is one test value per partition = 4 test cases.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — undercounts the partitions; there are 4, not 2.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — covers only the 3 valid partitions and forgets the invalid (negative) partition, which must also be exercised for 100% coverage.
option_notes.C: Correct — one test value from each of the 4 partitions (e.g., 500, 2500, 6000, -1).
option_notes.D: Incorrect — overcounts; EP requires one test per partition, not e.g. testing both ends of each range (that would be Boundary Value Analysis, a different technique).

questions.distractor_note: Option D is a common trap for readers who mentally blend EP with BVA — EP's coverage claim is 'one value per partition is enough because the whole partition behaves the same', not 'test every boundary'.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to identify how many partitions exist without asking for a test-case count, or ask you to pick which single test value set achieves 100% partition coverage.

questions.question: A shipping system should apply free shipping when orderValue <= 500. A developer accidentally implements this as 'if (orderValue == 500) applyFreeShipping()'. A tester derives 2-value BVA test data for this boundary: {500, 501}. Both tests pass their expected-vs-actual comparison despite the bug. Why did 2-value BVA fail to catch this defect, and what would catch it?

options.A: 2-value BVA is fundamentally broken and should never be used; only exploratory testing could catch this
options.B: The defect requires White-box statement coverage, since BVA cannot be used for this kind of boundary at all
options.C: 2-value BVA only exercises the boundary (500, correctly free under the bug) and its one adjacent neighbor (501, correctly not free under the bug); 3-value BVA would add the boundary's other neighbor (499), which SHOULD get free shipping per spec but wouldn't under the buggy '==' check, exposing the defect
options.D: The defect cannot be found by any black-box technique because it is a coding-level mistake

questions.why_correct: This mirrors the syllabus's own worked example almost exactly: for the boundary 'x <= 10' buggy-implemented as 'x = 10', 2-value BVA test data {10, 11} both accidentally pass under the bug, but 3-value BVA test data {9, 10, 11} adds 9, which exposes the defect since the buggy code incorrectly rejects it. Here, 499 is the value that should get free shipping (499 <= 500) but wouldn't under the '==' bug, exposing the mismatch between expected and actual results.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — overreaching conclusion; 2-value BVA is a valid, useful technique, it simply has lower fault-detection power than 3-value BVA for this specific defect pattern.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — BVA is precisely applicable to this ordered numeric boundary; white-box coverage is a different (structure-based) technique category and isn't required to catch this.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — this is exactly the kind of coding-level boundary defect black-box BVA is designed to expose from the outside, without knowledge of the implementation.

questions.alt_wording: May give you the buggy condition directly (e.g., 'if (x = 10)' instead of 'if (x <= 10)') and ask which BVA variant, or which specific input value, would detect the defect.

questions.question: A password-reset feature depends on two Boolean conditions: 'Email is registered' (T/F) and 'Account is locked' (T/F). All 4 combinations of these conditions are feasible and lead to distinct actions. Using a limited-entry decision table, what is the MINIMUM number of test cases needed to achieve 100% decision table coverage?

options.A: 2 test cases — one per condition
options.B: 3 test cases
options.C: 4 test cases — one per feasible column/rule
options.D: 8 test cases — covering every condition/action combination twice for confidence

questions.why_correct: In decision table testing, the coverage items are the columns containing feasible combinations of conditions (here, 2 conditions x 2 values each = 4 feasible rules/columns, since none are stated to be infeasible). 100% coverage requires exercising all feasible columns, i.e., one test case per rule — 4 test cases.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — confuses 'number of conditions' with 'number of coverage items (columns)'.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — undercounts; all 4 combinations here are feasible and must each be exercised.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — decision table coverage requires each feasible column at least once, not double-coverage; this also isn't how the syllabus defines 100% coverage for this technique.

questions.alt_wording: May instead give you a decision table with an infeasible ('N/A') combination and ask how many feasible columns remain, or describe simplification/merging of columns that don't affect the outcome.

questions.question: A document workflow has 3 states — Draft, Submitted, Approved — with 3 valid transitions: Draft->Submitted (submit), Submitted->Approved (approve), Submitted->Draft (reject). To achieve 100% valid transitions coverage (0-switch coverage), what is required, and how does it compare to 100% all states coverage?

options.A: Only the 3 states must each be visited at least once; visiting all states automatically guarantees all valid transitions have also been exercised
options.B: All 3 valid transitions must each be exercised at least once; achieving this guarantees full all states coverage is achieved too, but not vice versa
options.C: Only 1 test case is ever sufficient for both criteria, regardless of how many states or transitions exist
options.D: Valid transitions coverage additionally requires attempting invalid transitions such as Draft->Approved

questions.why_correct: Valid transitions (0-switch) coverage requires exercising all valid transitions (here, all 3). The syllabus states achieving full valid transitions coverage guarantees full all states coverage, but the reverse is not true — all states coverage is weaker and can typically be achieved without exercising every transition.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — reverses the guarantee direction; visiting all states does NOT guarantee all transitions were exercised (e.g., you could reach Approved without ever exercising the Submitted->Draft reject transition).
option_notes.C: Incorrect — while one well-designed test case sequence could coincidentally cover multiple transitions, this isn't guaranteed 'regardless of how many states or transitions exist', and is not a coverage rule from the syllabus.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — attempting invalid transitions is a requirement of ALL TRANSITIONS coverage, a stricter/different criterion, not valid transitions (0-switch) coverage.

questions.distractor_note: Option D deliberately blends 'all transitions coverage' (which does include attempted invalid transitions) into the definition of 'valid transitions coverage' (which only concerns the valid ones) — a realistic exam mix-up between the three named coverage criteria.
questions.alt_wording: May ask which coverage criterion 'should be a minimum requirement for mission and safety-critical software' (all transitions coverage, since it subsumes the other two).

questions.topic: Equivalence Partitioning vs. Boundary Value Analysis
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes Equivalence Partitioning (EP) from Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)?

options.A: EP can be applied to unordered, discrete partitions (e.g., a set of country codes), while BVA can only be used for ordered partitions since it needs a notion of 'boundary' and 'neighbor'
options.B: BVA is a black-box technique while EP is a white-box technique
options.C: EP always requires more test cases than BVA for the same input field
options.D: BVA can only be applied to numeric fields, while EP can only be applied to text fields

questions.why_correct: The syllabus explicitly states BVA can only be used for ordered partitions, because it exercises boundaries (minimum/maximum values) and requires the property that elements between two same-partition elements also belong to that partition — a notion that requires order. EP has no such restriction and applies to continuous or discrete, ordered or unordered partitions.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — both EP and BVA are black-box (specification-based) test techniques.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — there's no such general rule; the number of test cases depends on the number of partitions/boundaries in each specific case, not a fixed relationship between the two techniques.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — neither technique is restricted to only numeric or only text fields; partitions can be defined for many kinds of data elements, including inputs, outputs, configuration items and time-related values.

questions.alt_wording: May ask 'for which of the following fields could BVA NOT be meaningfully applied' and give an unordered set (e.g., a dropdown of unrelated category names) as the correct EXCEPT-style answer.

questions.question: A function contains 20 executable statements. A test suite exercises 17 of them, including the line 'result = total / count' but never with count equal to zero. What is the statement coverage achieved, and does it guarantee the division-by-zero defect will be found?

options.A: 85% coverage; yes, since the statement performing the division was executed, 100% statement coverage would guarantee the defect is found
options.B: 85% coverage; no — executing a statement does not guarantee all the data values that could expose a defect (like count = 0) were used
options.C: 100% coverage; no, statement coverage never relates to whether a specific statement was executed
options.D: 17% coverage; yes, because the statement was reached at all

questions.why_correct: Statement coverage = statements exercised / total executable statements = 17/20 = 85%. The syllabus explicitly warns that even 100% statement coverage will not detect defects that are data dependent, giving the exact example of a division by zero that only fails when the denominator is zero — exercising the statement with the wrong data still won't trigger the failure.

option_notes.A: Incorrect on both counts — the coverage percentage is right by coincidence-free math (17/20=85%) but the claim that 100% coverage guarantees finding this defect is explicitly contradicted by the syllabus's own division-by-zero example.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — wrong percentage (17/20 is 85%, not 100%), and statement coverage is by definition about which statements were executed.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — wrong percentage; also wrongly claims reaching the statement guarantees the defect is found regardless of data used.

questions.alt_wording: May give the same scenario and ask only for the coverage percentage (a pure calculation), or ask only about the data-dependency limitation without requiring the arithmetic.

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements:

I. Any test suite that achieves 100% branch coverage also achieves 100% statement coverage.
II. Any test suite that achieves 100% statement coverage also achieves 100% branch coverage.

Which is correct?

options.A: Only I is correct
options.B: Only II is correct
options.C: Both I and II are correct
options.D: Neither I nor II is correct

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states branch coverage subsumes statement coverage: achieving 100% branch coverage also achieves 100% statement coverage, but not vice versa. So statement I is true and statement II is false — you can reach every statement without having exercised both outcomes of every decision (e.g., an 'if' with no 'else' branch containing no unique statements).

option_notes.A: Correct — branch coverage is the stronger criterion and subsumes statement coverage, but the reverse doesn't hold.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — II is false; 100% statement coverage does not guarantee every branch (e.g., both true and false outcomes) was exercised.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — II is false.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — I is true.

questions.alt_wording: May ask directly: 'which coverage criterion is stronger/subsumes the other' or give a small code snippet and ask which coverage level a given test suite achieves.

questions.topic: Value and Limits of White-Box Testing
questions.question: A requirement states the system must lock a user account after 5 failed login attempts. The developer never implements this requirement at all. The team achieves 100% branch coverage on the login module through white-box testing. What BEST explains why this missing feature was not detected?

options.A: 100% branch coverage is impossible to achieve, so the team's coverage claim must be wrong
options.B: White-box testing takes the entire implementation into account, but if the software does not implement a requirement at all, there is no corresponding code to exercise, so white-box testing cannot detect this defect of omission
options.C: Branch coverage only applies to non-functional requirements, not functional ones like account lockout
options.D: The team should have used Equivalence Partitioning instead, which always finds every missing feature

questions.why_correct: This is a direct, named limitation in the syllabus: a weakness white-box test techniques share is that if the software does not implement one or more requirements, white-box testing may not detect the resulting defects of omission, since coverage measures are based on the code that exists, not on what SHOULD exist per the specification.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — 100% branch coverage of the code that does exist is entirely achievable; it just doesn't say anything about code that was never written.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — branch coverage is a structural/white-box measure applicable to any code, functional or non-functional; the issue here isn't the requirement type.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — EP is a black-box technique that also derives tests from what's specified, but it's not guaranteed to 'always find every missing feature' — no technique offers that guarantee, and this contradicts the absence-of-defects fallacy principle.

questions.alt_wording: May ask 'what is a fundamental weakness shared by all white-box test techniques' as a direct-definition question instead of a scenario.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes error guessing from exploratory testing?

options.A: Error guessing anticipates specific errors/defects/failures using prior knowledge (e.g., how the app failed before, common developer mistakes) to design targeted tests upfront; exploratory testing simultaneously designs, executes and evaluates tests while learning about the test object, often structured with test charters and time-boxed sessions
options.B: Error guessing and exploratory testing are two names for exactly the same technique
options.C: Exploratory testing always requires a fully detailed, pre-written test case for every test performed
options.D: Error guessing is a white-box technique, while exploratory testing is a black-box technique

questions.why_correct: Error guessing is anticipating errors/defects/failures based on the tester's knowledge (past application behavior, typical developer mistakes, failures in similar applications) to design targeted tests, often via 'fault attacks'. Exploratory testing instead simultaneously designs, executes, and evaluates tests while learning about the test object, frequently structured with session-based testing using test charters within a time box.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — they are two distinct experience-based techniques with different processes, though both rely on tester knowledge/skill.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — the defining feature of exploratory testing is the ABSENCE of fully pre-written test cases; tests are designed and executed together, in the moment.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — both are experience-based techniques, not white-box or black-box.

questions.alt_wording: May instead describe a 'fault attack' and ask which technique it belongs to (error guessing), or describe a 'test charter' and 'debriefing' and ask which technique that is (exploratory, session-based).

questions.question: A tester uses a list of high-level, experience-derived questions such as 'Are all error messages understandable to a non-technical user?' and 'Does every form field show a validation state?', checking each one directly against the application without following pre-scripted step-by-step test cases. Which technique is this?

options.A: Decision table testing
options.B: Checklist-based testing
options.C: State transition testing
options.D: Boundary value analysis

questions.why_correct: In checklist-based testing, a tester designs, implements, and executes tests to cover test conditions from a checklist, often phrased as questions that can be checked separately and directly — exactly matching the scenario, and built from experience or knowledge of why/how software fails.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — decision tables are built from combinations of Boolean/discrete conditions and actions, not open-ended experience-based questions.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — state transition testing is based on states/events/transitions, unrelated to a checklist of questions.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — BVA is a black-box, boundary-focused numeric technique, unrelated to this scenario.

questions.alt_wording: May emphasize that checklists 'should not contain items that can be checked automatically' or 'should be regularly updated based on defect analysis' as clues.

questions.topic: User Stories — The 3 C's and INVEST
questions.question: A user story's 'Confirmation' aspect, in the '3 C's' model (Card, Conversation, Confirmation), refers to:

options.A: The medium used to write the story down, such as an index card
options.B: The acceptance criteria that the implementation must meet
options.C: A verbal discussion about how the software will be used
options.D: The developer's sign-off that the code compiles

questions.why_correct: In the '3 C's' (Card, Conversation, Confirmation), Confirmation refers to the acceptance criteria — the conditions an implementation of the user story must meet to be accepted by stakeholders.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — that describes the Card aspect.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — that describes the Conversation aspect (can be documented or verbal).
option_notes.D: Incorrect — not part of the 3 C's model at all; Confirmation is about stakeholder acceptance criteria, not compilation.

questions.alt_wording: May ask you to name all three C's, or ask which INVEST letter ('Testable') relates most directly to writing good acceptance criteria.

questions.question: A team practicing ATDD has just finished a specification workshop resolving ambiguities in a new user story. What should they do NEXT, in the order the syllabus describes?

options.A: Immediately write non-functional performance tests, since those matter most for production readiness
options.B: Create the test cases based on the acceptance criteria — typically positive tests first (expected behavior with no errors), then negative tests, then non-functional characteristics
options.C: Automate every test case before any of them have been reviewed by the team
options.D: Skip straight to development, since the specification workshop already resolved all necessary ambiguity

questions.why_correct: After the specification workshop resolves incompleteness/ambiguity/defects in the user story, the next step is creating test cases from the acceptance criteria. The syllabus specifies the typical order: positive test cases first (confirming correct behavior without exceptions), then negative testing, and finally covering non-functional quality characteristics.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — non-functional characteristics are covered last, after positive and negative functional test cases, per the syllabus's stated order.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — automation happens as developers implement the feature and write supporting code, not necessarily before any team review, and isn't the immediate next step after the workshop.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — test case creation from the acceptance criteria still needs to happen before/alongside development; skipping it defeats the purpose of ATDD as a test-first approach.

questions.alt_wording: May ask you to put ATDD steps in order (specification workshop → test case creation → positive tests → negative tests → non-functional → automation as code is implemented) or ask which team members participate in creating the initial test cases (customers, developers, testers).

questions.question: All of the following are typical contents of a test plan, according to the syllabus, EXCEPT:

options.A: Context of testing, such as test scope, test objectives, and test basis
options.B: The risk register, including product and project risks
options.C: Budget and schedule
options.D: The full source code of the test object, embedded for reference

questions.why_correct: The syllabus's list of typical test plan content includes: context of testing, assumptions/constraints, stakeholders, communication, risk register, test approach, and budget/schedule. Embedding the full source code of the test object is not part of a test plan's typical content — a test plan documents the means and schedule for achieving test objectives, not the product's implementation itself.

option_notes.A: This IS typical test plan content — not the answer.
option_notes.B: This IS typical test plan content — not the answer.
option_notes.C: This IS typical test plan content — not the answer.
option_notes.D: Correct answer — not part of a test plan's typical content.

questions.alt_wording: May instead list content that belongs to a defect report or test completion report as the odd one out, testing whether you can tell these documents' typical contents apart.

questions.topic: Entry/Exit Criteria vs. Definition of Ready/Done
questions.question: In an Agile team, a user story must have clear acceptance criteria and available test data before development starts, and is only considered finished once all automated tests pass and the code has been reviewed. What are these two sets of conditions called, respectively, and which general concepts do they map to?

options.A: Definition of Ready maps to exit criteria; Definition of Done maps to entry criteria
options.B: Definition of Ready maps to entry criteria; Definition of Done maps to exit criteria
options.C: Both map to entry criteria; Agile has no equivalent of exit criteria
options.D: Both are informal terms with no relationship to entry/exit criteria at all

questions.why_correct: The syllabus explicitly states that in Agile software development, exit criteria are often called Definition of Done, and entry criteria that a user story must fulfill to start development/testing are called Definition of Ready. The 'must have criteria before starting' description matches entry criteria/Definition of Ready; the 'considered finished when' description matches exit criteria/Definition of Done.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — swapped; Ready is entry, Done is exit.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — Agile does have an equivalent of exit criteria (Definition of Done).
option_notes.D: Incorrect — the syllabus directly equates these terms with entry/exit criteria.

questions.alt_wording: May ask 'what happens if entry criteria are not met' (the activity is likely to prove more difficult, time-consuming, costly and riskier) as a related follow-up angle.

questions.question: Three experts estimate the effort for a test task using three-point estimation: optimistic (a) = 5 person-days, most likely (m) = 8 person-days, pessimistic (b) = 17 person-days. Using E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 and SD = (b - a) / 6, what is the final estimate and its range?

options.A: E = 10 person-days, range 8–12
options.B: E = 9 person-days, range 7–11
options.C: E = 8 person-days, range 5–17
options.D: E = 30 person-days, range 12–48

questions.why_correct: E = (5 + 4x8 + 17) / 6 = (5 + 32 + 17) / 6 = 54 / 6 = 9. SD = (17 - 5) / 6 = 12 / 6 = 2. So the estimate is 9 +/- 2 person-days, i.e., a range of 7 to 11 person-days.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — arithmetic error; recompute (5+32+17)/6 = 9, not 10.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — confuses the estimate with 'm' and the range with the raw (a, b) values instead of applying the SD formula.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — forgets to divide by 6 in one or both formulas.

questions.alt_wording: May give different a/m/b numbers, ask only for E, or ask only for SD/the range — always apply E = (a+4m+b)/6 and SD = (b-a)/6 carefully with the given numbers.

questions.question: A team orders its test execution schedule so that the test case exercising the greatest number of NOT-yet-covered statements runs next, repeating this logic for each subsequent test case. Which prioritization strategy is this?

options.A: Risk-based prioritization
options.B: Requirements-based prioritization
options.C: Coverage-based prioritization (specifically, additional coverage prioritization)
options.D: Random prioritization based on resource availability only

questions.why_correct: This is exactly the syllabus's description of additional coverage prioritization, a variant of coverage-based prioritization: the test case achieving the highest coverage runs first, and each subsequent test case is the one achieving the highest ADDITIONAL coverage beyond what's already been covered.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — risk-based prioritization orders execution by risk analysis results, not by incremental statement coverage.
option_notes.B: Incorrect — requirements-based prioritization orders execution by stakeholder-defined requirement priority, not coverage.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — resource availability is a real scheduling constraint the syllabus mentions, but it's not itself a named prioritization strategy, and doesn't match the 'not-yet-covered statements' description.

questions.alt_wording: May instead describe test cases being run in order of the most business-critical requirement first (requirements-based) or in order of highest identified risk first (risk-based).

questions.question: In the testing quadrants model, automated component tests included in the CI process belong to which quadrant, and how does it differ from the quadrant containing manual exploratory and user acceptance testing?

options.A: Both belong to Quadrant Q1 (technology-facing, supports the team); there is no meaningful difference
options.B: Component tests belong to Q1 (technology-facing, supports the team); exploratory/UAT belong to Q3 (business-facing, critiques the product)
options.C: Component tests belong to Q3 (business-facing, critiques the product); exploratory/UAT belong to Q1 (technology-facing, supports the team)
options.D: Component tests belong to Q4 (technology-facing, critiques the product); exploratory/UAT belong to Q2 (business-facing, supports the team)

questions.why_correct: Quadrant Q1 (technology-facing, supports the team) contains component tests and component integration tests, which should be automated and included in CI. Quadrant Q3 (business-facing, critiques the product) contains exploratory testing, usability testing, and user acceptance testing — user-oriented and often manual, as described.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — the two test types described belong to different quadrants (Q1 vs Q3) with a real distinction.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — the two quadrant assignments are reversed.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — mismatches both test types to the wrong quadrants; Q4 is technology-facing/critique (smoke tests, non-functional except usability) and Q2 is business-facing/support-the-team (functional tests, user story tests, API testing).

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which quadrant contains 'smoke tests and non-functional tests (except usability)' (Q4) or which quadrant contains 'functional tests, examples, API testing' (Q2).

questions.question: Feature X has a high likelihood of failure and a high impact if it fails. Feature Y has a low likelihood of failure but also a high impact if it fails. According to the syllabus's definition of risk level, which feature has the higher risk level and should receive more test attention first?

options.A: Feature Y, because impact matters more than likelihood
options.B: Feature X, because risk level is a function of both risk likelihood and risk impact, and X is high on both while Y is only high on one
options.C: Both are equal, since impact is identical
options.D: Neither can be prioritized without knowing the exact budget

questions.why_correct: Risk level is expressed by combining risk likelihood (probability of occurrence) and risk impact (harm/consequences); the higher the risk level, the more important its treatment. Feature X is high on both factors, giving it a higher overall risk level than Feature Y, which is high on only one factor.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — risk level depends on both factors together, not impact alone.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — equal impact does not mean equal risk level, since likelihood also differs.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — budget affects how you RESPOND to risk (mitigation options), not the underlying risk level calculation itself, which is based on likelihood and impact.

questions.alt_wording: May give qualitative categories (e.g., a risk matrix with High/Medium/Low cells) instead of a direct comparison, and ask you to identify the cell representing the highest risk level.

questions.question: A test manager identifies two concerns: (1) the third-party analytics vendor may go out of business before launch, and (2) the search feature sometimes returns incorrect results for queries containing special characters. How should these be classified?

options.A: Both are product risks, since both could affect the release
options.B: (1) is a project risk (supplier issue); (2) is a product risk (incorrect functionality)
options.C: (1) is a product risk; (2) is a project risk
options.D: Both are project risks, since a manager identified them

questions.why_correct: Project risks relate to management/control of the project, including supplier issues such as third-party delivery failure or vendor bankruptcy — matching concern (1) exactly. Product risks relate to product quality characteristics, including missing/wrong functionality — matching concern (2), the search feature returning incorrect results.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — conflates two categories with different natures; a vendor going out of business is a project-management concern, not a product quality characteristic.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — reversed.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — who identifies a risk has no bearing on its classification; classification depends on whether the risk concerns project management/control or the product's own quality characteristics.

questions.alt_wording: May list other project-risk examples (insufficient skills, scope creep, cost cutting) or product-risk examples (poor architecture, inadequate response time, security vulnerabilities) and ask you to sort them.

questions.question: Which of the following is an action the syllabus lists for mitigating a product risk THROUGH TESTING?

options.A: Transferring the risk to an insurance provider
options.B: Applying an appropriate level of independence of testing and performing reviews and static analysis
options.C: Accepting the risk without any further action
options.D: Removing the feature from scope entirely

questions.why_correct: The syllabus's list of testing-based product risk mitigation actions includes: selecting testers with the right experience/skills, applying an appropriate level of independence of testing, performing reviews and static analysis, applying appropriate test techniques/coverage/test types, and performing dynamic testing including regression testing.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — risk transfer is a general risk-response option, but it is not a testing-based mitigation action.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — risk acceptance is a general response option (doing nothing further), not a testing-based mitigation.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — removing scope is a project-level decision, not a testing activity.

questions.alt_wording: May ask you to distinguish testing-based mitigation actions from the general risk-response options (mitigation, acceptance, transfer, contingency plan) that apply beyond just testing.

questions.question: 'Mean time to failure' and 'availability' are examples of which category of test metric, and how does that differ from 'number of test cases run/not run, passed/failed'?

options.A: Both are the same category: defect metrics
options.B: 'Mean time to failure'/'availability' are product quality metrics; 'test cases run/passed/failed' are test progress metrics
options.C: 'Mean time to failure'/'availability' are test progress metrics; 'test cases run/passed/failed' are product quality metrics
options.D: Both are coverage metrics, just measured differently

questions.why_correct: The syllabus lists product quality metrics (e.g., availability, response time, mean time to failure) as a distinct category from test progress metrics (e.g., test case implementation progress, number of test cases run/not run, passed/failed, test execution time).

option_notes.A: Incorrect — defect metrics are yet another distinct category (e.g., number/priority of defects found/fixed, defect density).
option_notes.C: Incorrect — reversed.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — coverage metrics are a separate category (e.g., requirements coverage, code coverage), matching neither example given.

questions.alt_wording: May list a metric from a different category (e.g., 'cost of testing' = cost metric, or 'residual risk level' = risk metric) and ask you to classify it.

questions.topic: Test Progress Reports vs. Test Completion Reports
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a test progress report from a test completion report?

options.A: A test progress report is generated once, at project end; a test completion report is generated daily or weekly throughout testing
options.B: A test progress report is generated regularly (e.g., daily/weekly) to support ongoing test control; a test completion report summarizes a specific completed test activity (e.g., a test level or iteration) against the original test plan, once it is done
options.C: Both reports contain identical content and are simply named differently depending on the organization
options.D: Only the test completion report includes any information about risks; test progress reports never mention risk

questions.why_correct: Test progress reports are usually generated on a regular basis to support ongoing test control, informing stakeholders of progress, impediments, metrics, and risks. A test completion report is instead prepared during test completion, summarizing a specific test activity's results against the original test plan (objectives and exit criteria), typically only once per milestone.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — the frequencies are reversed.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — they have different typical content (e.g., completion reports include deviations from the plan and lessons learned; progress reports focus on ongoing status and near-term plans) and different frequency/purpose.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — test progress reports also explicitly include 'new and changed risks within the testing period'.

questions.alt_wording: May ask which report 'uses test progress reports and other data as input' (test completion report) or which is described by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 as a 'test status report' (progress report).

questions.question: A team needs to reproduce a defect that was only observed against last month's version of the test environment. Which practice makes this possible?

options.A: Risk-based testing
options.B: Configuration management, which allows reverting to a previous approved baseline
options.C: Test case prioritization
options.D: Checklist-based testing

questions.why_correct: Configuration management (CM) provides a discipline for identifying, controlling, and tracking work products as configuration items, recording changed items when a new baseline is created; it is explicitly possible to revert to a previous baseline to reproduce previous test results.

option_notes.A: Incorrect — risk-based testing is about prioritizing test effort by risk, unrelated to reverting environment versions.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — test case prioritization is about execution order, not environment version control.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — checklist-based testing is an experience-based test design technique, unrelated to configuration/version tracking.

questions.alt_wording: May describe CM's role as ensuring 'configuration items are uniquely identified, version controlled, tracked for changes, and related to other configuration items' for traceability instead of the reproduction angle.

questions.question: A defect report logged during dynamic testing typically includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Expected results and actual results
options.B: Severity of the defect and priority to fix
options.C: Status of the defect (e.g., open, deferred, awaiting confirmation testing, closed)
options.D: The confirmed root cause of the defect as determined by root cause analysis

questions.why_correct: The syllabus's list of typical defect report fields includes a unique identifier, title, date/author/role, test object/environment identification, context, a description enabling reproduction, expected vs. actual results, severity, priority, status, and references. Root cause is not among these fields — root cause analysis is a separate activity (see section 1.2.3) typically performed afterward, not a standard field logged on the initial defect report itself.

option_notes.A: This IS a typical defect report field — not the answer.
option_notes.B: This IS a typical defect report field — not the answer.
option_notes.C: This IS a typical defect report field — not the answer.
option_notes.D: Correct answer — not part of the syllabus's listed defect report content.

questions.alt_wording: May instead list 'unique identifier', 'context of the defect', or 'references (e.g., to the test case)' among the options and ask you to spot a fabricated field instead.

questions.topic: Benefits and Risks of Test Automation
questions.question: A manager decides to automate all regression tests and, based on this, tells stakeholders that manual testers are no longer needed at all and that the automated suite guarantees defect-free releases. Which risk of test automation does this BEST illustrate?

options.A: The automation tool is incompatible with the development platform
options.B: Unrealistic expectations about the benefits of a tool, and relying on it too much, ignoring the need for human critical thinking
options.C: The dependency on a tool vendor that may go out of business
options.D: Choosing a tool that doesn't comply with regulatory requirements

questions.why_correct: This scenario matches two of the syllabus's explicitly listed test automation risks: unrealistic expectations about the benefits of a tool, and relying on a tool too much, e.g., ignoring the need for human critical thinking (assuming automation alone guarantees defect-free software also contradicts the absence-of-defects fallacy principle).

option_notes.A: Incorrect — no platform-compatibility issue is described in the scenario.
option_notes.C: Incorrect — no vendor dependency issue is described.
option_notes.D: Incorrect — no regulatory/compliance issue is described.

questions.alt_wording: May instead describe a team underestimating the time/cost/effort to introduce and maintain a tool (a different listed risk) or ask for a genuine BENEFIT of automation as a contrast (e.g., 'more time for testers to design new, deeper tests').

questions.question: A team needs to simulate 20,000 concurrent users placing orders through an e-commerce checkout. The behavior would be difficult and unreliable to perform manually. Which type of test tool support BEST fits this need?

options.A: Static testing tools
options.B: Non-functional testing tools
options.C: Collaboration tools
options.D: Test management tools

questions.why_correct: The syllabus lists non-functional testing tools as tools that allow testers to perform non-functional testing that is difficult or impossible to perform manually. Simulating many concurrent users is a typical performance/load-testing situation, so non-functional test tool support is the best fit.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - static testing tools support reviews and static analysis, not dynamic load simulation.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - collaboration tools facilitate communication; they do not generate load or measure performance behavior.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - test management tools help manage requirements, tests, defects, configuration, and related test process information, but they are not the direct tool type for load simulation.

questions.alt_wording: May ask which tool type supports performance, security, reliability, or other non-functional testing that would be hard to do manually.

questions.topic: What Counts as a Test Tool
questions.question: Which statement is FALSE according to the syllabus section on tool support for testing?

options.A: Test management tools can facilitate management of requirements, tests, defects, and configuration.
options.B: DevOps tools can support the delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated build processes, and CI/CD.
options.C: A spreadsheet cannot be considered a test tool because it is not a dedicated testing product.
options.D: Test design and test implementation tools can facilitate generation of test cases, test data, and test procedures.

questions.why_correct: The syllabus explicitly allows a broad definition: any tool that assists in testing can be considered a test tool, and it gives a spreadsheet as an example in the testing context. A tool does not need to be a dedicated commercial testing product to support testing.

option_notes.A: True - this matches the syllabus description of test management tools.
option_notes.B: True - this matches the syllabus description of DevOps tools.
option_notes.C: Correct answer - this statement is false.
option_notes.D: True - this matches the syllabus description of test design and implementation tools.

questions.distractor_note: The tempting mistake is to interpret 'test tool' too narrowly. CTFL uses a functional definition: if it assists testing, it can count in that context.
questions.alt_wording: May be phrased as 'which of these could be a test tool in context?' with spreadsheet, checklist, collaboration board, or pipeline tool as possible examples.

questions.topic: State Transition Testing - All Transitions Coverage
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about state transition testing:

I. All transitions coverage requires test cases to exercise all valid transitions and attempt invalid transitions shown in a state table.
II. Testing several invalid transitions in one test case is preferred because it reduces defect masking.

Which is correct?

options.A: Only I is correct
options.B: Only II is correct
options.C: Both I and II are correct
options.D: Neither I nor II is correct

questions.why_correct: Statement I matches the syllabus: all transitions coverage covers both valid and invalid transitions. Statement II is false because the syllabus recommends testing only one invalid transition in a single test case to help avoid defect masking, where one defect prevents detection of another.

option_notes.A: Correct - I is true and II is false.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - II reverses the syllabus guidance on invalid transitions.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - II is false.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - I is true.

questions.distractor_note: Combining invalid transitions can sound efficient, but CTFL cares about diagnostic clarity. One invalid transition per test case makes it easier to see which transition caused the observed behavior.
questions.alt_wording: May ask about all states coverage, valid transitions coverage (0-switch), or all transitions coverage; read whether invalid transitions are included.

questions.question: An input field accepts whole-number quantities from 1 through 10 inclusive. Using 3-value boundary value analysis, which set of values gives 100% boundary coverage for this single valid range and its adjacent invalid partitions?
questions.why_correct: In 3-value BVA, each boundary has three coverage items: the boundary value and both of its closest neighbors. For the lower boundary 1, the values are 0, 1, and 2. For the upper boundary 10, the values are 9, 10, and 11. Together this gives 0, 1, 2, 9, 10, and 11.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - this exercises only the exact boundary values, not their neighbors.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - this is closer to 2-value BVA, not 3-value BVA.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - it omits the adjacent invalid neighbors 0 and 11.

questions.alt_wording: May ask for 2-value BVA instead; for this same range, 2-value BVA would use the boundary values and the closest neighbors in adjacent partitions: 0, 1, 10, and 11.

questions.question: A minimized decision table has 8 feasible decision rules. During testing, test cases exercise 6 of those feasible rules. What is the decision table coverage?
questions.why_correct: In decision table testing, the coverage items are the columns containing feasible combinations of conditions. Coverage is the number of exercised feasible columns divided by the total number of feasible columns. Here, 6 / 8 = 0.75 = 75%.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - this treats the number of exercised rules as the percentage.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - this is the uncovered portion, 2 out of 8, not the exercised coverage.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - 100% would require exercising all 8 feasible rules.

questions.alt_wording: May ask how many additional test cases or rules are needed to reach 100% coverage, or may mention feasible columns instead of decision rules.

questions.question: A user story's acceptance criteria are written as a table mapping account status and payment status to whether access should be granted. Which acceptance-criteria format is this, and how does it differ from Given/When/Then?

options.A: Scenario-oriented; Given/When/Then is rule-oriented
options.B: Rule-oriented; Given/When/Then is scenario-oriented
options.C: Exploratory; Given/When/Then is checklist-based
options.D: Static analysis; Given/When/Then is dynamic testing

questions.why_correct: The syllabus gives two common acceptance criteria formats: scenario-oriented, such as Given/When/Then, and rule-oriented, such as a bullet point verification list or a tabulated input-output mapping. A table mapping inputs to expected outputs is rule-oriented.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - the two formats are reversed.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - exploratory and checklist-based testing are experience-based test techniques, not the two acceptance-criteria formats named here.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - these are not acceptance-criteria formats.

questions.distractor_note: Given/When/Then often gets associated with BDD and scenarios. A table of rules may still be excellent acceptance criteria, but it is rule-oriented rather than scenario-oriented.
questions.alt_wording: May describe rule-oriented criteria as a verification list, decision table-like mapping, or input-output table.

questions.question: A team uses ATDD for a user story about applying a discount code at checkout. Which test case is LEAST appropriate to include for that story?

options.A: A positive test showing a valid discount code reduces the order total.
options.B: A negative test showing an expired discount code is rejected with a clear message.
options.C: A usability-related acceptance test checking that the discount error message is understandable to the shopper.
options.D: An end-to-end test of the warehouse picking workflow after the order is shipped.

questions.why_correct: ATDD test cases are based on the acceptance criteria, should cover all characteristics of the user story, and should not go beyond the story. Positive, negative, and relevant non-functional characteristics may be included. A warehouse picking workflow after shipment is outside the discount-code checkout story.

option_notes.A: Appropriate - ATDD typically starts with positive tests for expected behavior.
option_notes.B: Appropriate - after positive tests, the team should perform negative testing.
option_notes.C: Appropriate if message understandability is part of the story or acceptance criteria; the syllabus allows relevant non-functional characteristics such as usability.
option_notes.D: Correct answer - least appropriate because it goes beyond the user story's scope.

questions.alt_wording: May ask which ATDD test case goes beyond the story, duplicates another characteristic, or is not understandable to stakeholders.

questions.question: An organization has historical data showing a development-to-test effort ratio of 5:2 for similar projects. The new project is estimated at 750 person-days of development effort. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the estimated test effort?

options.A: 150 person-days
options.B: 300 person-days
options.C: 375 person-days
options.D: 1,875 person-days

questions.why_correct: A development-to-test ratio of 5:2 means test effort is 2/5 of development effort. 750 x 2/5 = 300 person-days. This matches the syllabus example pattern for ratio-based estimation using historical organizational data.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - this uses 1/5 rather than 2/5.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - this uses 1/2 of development effort, not the 5:2 ratio.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - this multiplies by 5/2 instead of 2/5.

questions.alt_wording: May phrase the ratio as 'for every 5 days of development, 2 days of testing were needed' or use a different historical development-to-test ratio.

questions.question: A high-priority end-to-end payment test depends on a lower-priority account setup test because the payment cannot be attempted until a verified account exists. What should the test execution schedule do?

options.A: Run the high-priority payment test first because priority always overrides dependencies.
options.B: Run the lower-priority setup test first because the higher-priority test depends on it.
options.C: Skip the setup test because it is lower priority.
options.D: Run both tests randomly because dependencies are not considered in prioritization.

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states that ideal priority ordering may not work when test cases or features have dependencies. If a higher-priority test case depends on a lower-priority test case, the lower-priority test case must be executed first.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - priority matters, but dependencies can constrain execution order.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - skipping the prerequisite would prevent the dependent test from being executed meaningfully.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - dependencies and resource availability are explicitly considered when arranging the test execution schedule.

questions.distractor_note: This question checks whether you treat prioritization as a real schedule, not just a sorted list. Dependencies can force a lower-priority test to run earlier.
questions.alt_wording: May mention resource availability instead of dependencies, such as an environment or specialist tester available only during a specific time window.

questions.question: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between lower and higher layers in the test pyramid?

options.A: Lower-layer tests are usually larger, slower, and less isolated than higher-layer tests.
options.B: Higher-layer tests usually have lower granularity, lower isolation, and longer execution time than lower-layer tests.
options.C: The top layer should contain the largest number of small component tests.
options.D: The test pyramid is only about manual testing and does not support automation decisions.

questions.why_correct: The syllabus describes the test pyramid as a model showing different test granularities. Higher layers have lower granularity, lower isolation, and higher execution time. Bottom-layer tests are small, isolated, fast, and numerous; top-layer tests are complex, high-level, end-to-end, slower, and fewer.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - this reverses the pyramid characteristics.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - small component-level tests belong near the bottom, not the top.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the model supports teams in test automation and test effort allocation.

questions.alt_wording: May ask why many fast component tests and fewer end-to-end tests are generally expected in a pyramid-shaped test strategy.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:

I. Availability of test data and a configured test environment are typical entry criteria.
II. Achieved coverage level and number of unresolved defects are typical exit criteria.
III. Running out of time or budget can never be treated as an exit criterion.

Which statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and III only
options.D: I, II, and III

questions.why_correct: Entry criteria define preconditions for starting an activity, such as availability of resources, environments, test data, budget, and testware. Exit criteria define what must be achieved to declare completion, such as achieved coverage, unresolved defect levels, or failed test counts. Statement III is false because the syllabus says running out of time or budget can also be viewed as valid exit criteria if stakeholders review and accept the release risk.

option_notes.A: Correct - I and II are true; III is false.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - I is true and III is false.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - III is false.

questions.distractor_note: Statement III sounds like a quality-first rule, but CTFL recognizes business constraints. Ending due to time or budget is acceptable only with stakeholder risk acceptance.
questions.alt_wording: May use Agile terms: Definition of Ready aligns with entry criteria, while Definition of Done aligns with exit criteria.

questions.question: A small function has 10 executable statements and 6 branches. A test suite executes all 10 statements and 4 of the 6 branches. What can be concluded?

options.A: Statement coverage is 100% and branch coverage is approximately 67%.
options.B: Statement coverage is approximately 67% and branch coverage is 100%.
options.C: Both statement coverage and branch coverage are 100%.
options.D: Branch coverage cannot be measured unless statement coverage is below 100%.

questions.why_correct: Statement coverage is the number of executed statements divided by the total executable statements: 10/10 = 100%. Branch coverage is the number of executed branches divided by the total branches: 4/6 = 66.7%, approximately 67%. Achieving 100% statement coverage does not necessarily mean 100% branch coverage.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - the two coverage measures are reversed.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - branch coverage is not 100% because only 4 of 6 branches were exercised.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - branch coverage can be measured independently and is stronger than statement coverage.

questions.distractor_note: The key trap is assuming that executing every statement automatically exercises every branch outcome. CTFL expects you to keep statement and branch coverage separate.
questions.alt_wording: May ask whether 100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage. In the syllabus, 100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage, but not the other way around.
